title: Tomato identity and growth habit
content: Tomato is Solanum lycopersicum, also published under the older name Lycopersicon lycopersicum. It is a heat-loving crop grown through a frost-free season, with bush and vining forms that differ in support needs and fruiting pattern.
cautions: A common name or photograph alone may not establish a cultivar.

title: Tomatoes need a sunny, uncrowded site
content: Tomatoes perform best in full sun. Give plants enough space for air movement and provide a support appropriate to the variety. Low light, crowding, and excessive leafy growth can all contribute to slow or incomplete fruit ripening.
cautions: Local climate and cultivar growth habit affect spacing and support choices.

title: Keep tomato soil moisture consistent
content: Water tomatoes thoroughly enough to moisten the root zone, then use soil conditions rather than a calendar to decide when to water again. Large moisture swings during fruit development are associated with blossom-end rot and growth cracking; frequent shallow watering promotes shallow roots.
cautions: Rainfall, soil texture, containers, and weather change water demand.
Blossom-end rot has interacting causes and should not be diagnosed from watering history alone.

title: Visible pattern associated with Septoria leaf spot
content: Septoria leaf spot commonly begins on lower tomato leaves as numerous small, round gray spots with darker margins. Spots can enlarge and merge as leaves yellow and die, especially during wet weather. Similar spotting can occur for other reasons, so confirm before acting.
cautions: A photograph alone cannot confirm a fungal pathogen.
Seek a local extension or plant diagnostic service when symptoms are severe or unclear.

title: Visible pattern associated with early blight
content: Early blight often starts on older, lower tomato leaves as irregular brown lesions that may have yellow margins and concentric rings. Enlarging lesions can merge and kill leaves, and fruit may sometimes rot. Septoria and other disorders can overlap visually, so use more than one symptom for assessment.
cautions: Do not treat a visual pattern as a confirmed diagnosis.
Ask a local extension service about region-appropriate management.

title: Bacterial spot can affect leaves and fruit
content: Bacterial spot can produce small dark spots on tomato leaves and fruit. Leaf spots may merge as affected leaves yellow, brown, and drop. These signs overlap with several fungal and environmental problems, so laboratory or local extension confirmation may be needed.
cautions: Avoid declaring bacterial disease from an image alone.
Wet conditions can favor several different tomato diseases.

title: Mosaic-like distortion requires confirmation
content: Tomato mosaic viruses may be associated with twisted, curled, rough, crinkled, or unusually small leaves and irregular color patterns on foliage or fruit. Herbicide exposure, insects, and environmental stress may also distort leaves, so these signs are not diagnostic by themselves.
cautions: Consult a plant diagnostic service before concluding that a virus is present.

title: Check curled or sticky tomato leaves for aphids
content: Aphids can gather in large numbers on tomato plants and may be associated with curled, discolored, or sticky leaves. Inspect tender growth and leaf undersides for the insects and for beneficial predators before deciding whether intervention is needed.
cautions: Curling and discoloration also occur with water, heat, virus, and spray injury.

title: Cucurbita pepo pumpkin identity
content: Cucurbita pepo is an accepted species that includes cultivated forms called pumpkins as well as some squashes and gourds. It is generally a trailing annual vine with separate pollen-bearing and fruit-bearing flowers on the same plant.
cautions: The common name pumpkin is also used for cultivated forms of other Cucurbita species.

title: Pothos identity and useful distinguishing features
content: Pothos is Epipremnum aureum, a climbing or trailing evergreen in the arum family. It was previously called Scindapsus aureus and E. pinnatum 'Aureum'. Glossy, often heart-shaped leaves, grooved leaf stalks, and brown aerial roots help distinguish it from heartleaf philodendron.
cautions: Cultivar color and variegation vary, so foliage color alone is not a reliable identification.

title: Pothos prefers bright indirect light
content: Pothos prefers bright, indirect light but can remain alive for long periods in lower light. Low light may reduce variegation, while harsh direct sun can injure foliage. Changes in cultivar pattern should be compared with new and older leaves before assuming stress.
cautions: Variegation differs naturally among cultivars.

title: Let pothos potting mix dry between watering
content: Allow a well-drained pothos potting medium to dry between waterings, then water according to the actual moisture in the container. Pot size, light, temperature, season, and root density all alter drying time, so a fixed calendar is unreliable.
cautions: Do not leave the root zone continuously saturated.

title: Use a well-drained medium for pothos
content: Pothos needs a potting medium and container that allow excess water to drain. A high-organic-matter loam or suitable houseplant medium can work when it remains aerated rather than waterlogged. Assess the whole container system, not soil ingredients in isolation.
cautions: Containers without drainage increase the risk of persistent saturation.

title: Persistent moisture raises pothos root-rot risk
content: Overwatering or poor drainage can lead to pothos root rot and blackened leaf margins. Yellowing alone is not specific: normal leaf aging, low light, and other root problems can look similar. Check pot drainage, root condition, and moisture history together.
cautions: Do not diagnose root rot from leaf color alone.

title: Pothos tolerates homes but benefits from humidity
content: Pothos is adaptable indoors and can benefit from increased humidity. Humidity should not be considered separately from air movement, temperature, light, and watering because overly wet media remains a greater root risk than ordinary household air.
cautions: A pebble tray must not leave the pot standing in water.

title: Monitor pothos for mealybugs and scale
content: Pothos can host mealybugs and scale insects. Inspect leaf undersides, stems, nodes, and new growth when leaves become sticky, discolored, or weak. Isolate a newly affected plant while confirming the pest to reduce spread through an indoor collection.
cautions: Use an identified pest and product label, not symptoms alone, to guide any treatment.

title: Pothos contains irritating calcium oxalate crystals
content: All parts of pothos contain calcium oxalate crystals and are considered poisonous to people and pets. Chewing may cause mouth pain or swelling, drooling, vomiting, difficulty swallowing, or skin irritation. Keep the plant away from children and animals that may chew it.
cautions: Contact a poison-control center or veterinarian promptly after suspected ingestion or significant symptoms.

title: Snake plant and its older scientific name
content: Snake plant is Dracaena trifasciata, formerly Sansevieria trifasciata. It is a clumping evergreen with stiff, upright, sword-shaped leaves that arise from the base and commonly show horizontal green banding. Cultivars vary widely in size and variegation.
cautions: Cultivar markings alone do not prove species identity.

title: Snake plants tolerate low light but avoid harsh sun
content: Snake plants tolerate very low light but generally prefer a warm, bright location with indirect or limited direct light. Protect foliage from intense afternoon sun, which can scorch leaves. Growth rate and water use usually decrease in dimmer conditions.
cautions: Move plants gradually when changing light exposure.

title: Let snake plant soil dry between watering
content: Allow snake plant soil to dry between waterings and reduce watering substantially during the low-growth winter period. Check moisture below the surface before adding water. The interval will vary with light, season, pot material, root density, and temperature.
cautions: Do not pour water into the center of the leaf rosette.
A calendar interval cannot replace checking the soil.

title: Snake plant roots require good drainage
content: Use a well-draining potting mix and a container that releases excess water. Snake plants tolerate dry soil better than persistent saturation. Stable, wider containers may help support tall leaves, but drainage remains more important than container shape.
cautions: A decorative outer pot should not trap water around the growing container.

title: Overwatering is a major snake plant risk
content: Persistent wetness can rot snake plant roots. Yellowing, soft tissue, poor anchorage, or decline alongside wet soil increases concern, but those signs are not individually diagnostic. Inspect drainage and roots and rule out cold injury or other damage.
cautions: Severely rotted roots may require assessment by an experienced horticulturist.

title: Snake plant is tropical and frost-sensitive
content: Snake plant is a tropical perennial normally kept indoors outside warm climates. It tolerates cool indoor conditions better than many tropical plants, but should be protected from frost and abrupt cold exposure. Cooler, dimmer conditions also reduce water use.
cautions: Bring container plants indoors before local frost risk.

title: Occasional pests of snake plant
content: Snake plants have few major pest problems, but mealybugs and spider mites may occur. Inspect leaf bases, both leaf surfaces, and nearby plants for insects, cottony material, fine webbing, or stippling before concluding that discoloration is pest-related.
cautions: Identify the pest before using any pesticide and follow the product label.

title: Snake plant contains saponins
content: Snake plant contains saponins and is considered toxic if eaten, including for cats and dogs. Reported signs include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, drooling, appetite loss, or depression; sap may irritate skin. Keep it away from children and animals likely to chew plants.
cautions: Contact a poison-control center or veterinarian promptly after suspected ingestion or significant symptoms.

title: Peace lily identity and flower structure
content: Spathiphyllum wallisii is a compact member of the peace-lily group. Peace lilies form basal clumps of glossy dark-green leaves. Their familiar white 'flower' includes a leaf-like spathe surrounding a central spadix and may age from white toward green.
cautions: Many Spathiphyllum species and cultivars share the peace lily name.

title: Peace lilies prefer filtered light
content: Peace lilies tolerate lower-light locations but prefer bright filtered light and should be kept out of direct sun. Excessive direct light can contribute to brown tips or scorched foliage, while flowering and growth may be reduced in very dim conditions.
cautions: Brown tips have several possible causes, including water stress and low humidity.

title: Peace lily soil should be moist, not soggy
content: Keep peace lily soil evenly moist but not saturated, allowing some drying between waterings without prolonged wilting. Check the potting medium rather than relying on a fixed schedule. Bottom watering can work when excess water is not left around the roots.
cautions: Wilting can reflect either dry roots or damaged roots in persistently wet soil.

title: Peace lilies need moisture with drainage
content: Peace lilies prefer a potting mix rich in organic matter that holds useful moisture while still draining well. They may grow well somewhat pot-bound, so repot because roots or medium condition require it rather than automatically moving to an oversized container.
cautions: An oversized volume of wet mix can remain saturated longer than the root system can use.

title: Protect peace lilies from cold and drafts
content: Peace lilies prefer warm indoor conditions. Cool drafts and sustained temperatures in the lower indoor range slow growth, while extended exposure near or below 40°F can damage leaves, stems, and roots. Keep plants away from cold windows and outdoor frost.
cautions: Temperature injury can resemble watering or root problems.

title: Peace lilies have low fertilizer needs
content: Indoor peace lilies have relatively low fertility needs. Excess fertilizer and accumulated salts can burn leaf tips and roots. Base any feeding on active growth, product directions, and the condition of the potting medium rather than assuming pale or brown foliage proves deficiency.
cautions: Do not exceed label directions.
Leaf-tip burn is not specific to fertilizer salts.

title: Inspect peace lilies for mealybugs and scale
content: Mealybugs are a common indoor pest of peace lilies, and scale can also occur. Inspect broad leaf surfaces, undersides, bases, and new growth for insects or residue. Regularly wiping leaves can remove dust and some pests while making inspection easier.
cautions: Identify the pest before choosing a control and follow any product label.

title: Peace lily leaves contain calcium oxalate crystals
content: Peace lily leaves contain calcium oxalate crystals and can be poisonous if eaten, including by pets. Reported signs include mouth pain or burning, drooling, vomiting, and difficulty swallowing. Keep the plant away from children and animals likely to chew foliage.
cautions: Contact a poison-control center or veterinarian promptly after suspected ingestion or significant symptoms.

title: Pumpkins need warmth, sun, drainage, and room
content: Pumpkins prefer a sunny location with fertile, well-drained soil and room for vines. Planting into cold soil or disturbing roots during transplanting can slow establishment. Row covers can shelter young plants, but must come off at flowering so pollinators can reach blooms.
cautions: Planting dates and spacing vary with climate and cultivar.

title: Water pumpkin roots deeply and assess the soil
content: Pumpkins benefit from deep watering that reaches the root zone, with mulch helping conserve moisture. Prefer drip or base watering where practical so foliage stays drier. Judge timing from soil, rainfall, temperature, and growth rather than applying a universal schedule.
cautions: Containers, soil texture, rainfall, and heat can substantially change water demand.

title: Powdery mildew pattern on pumpkin foliage
content: Powdery mildew on cucurbits appears as white powdery patches on upper or lower leaf surfaces, often beginning on older leaves in warm, humid weather. It can spread until foliage yellows and dies, exposing developing fruit to stronger sunlight.
cautions: Some cucurbits have normal silvery leaf markings without powdery residue.
Confirm the cause before selecting any control.

title: Downy mildew differs from powdery mildew
content: Cucurbit downy mildew is associated with angular yellow or tan lesions on upper leaf surfaces and grayish growth beneath them. Lesions can merge as leaves yellow and die in humid conditions. Unlike powdery mildew, the visible growth is usually concentrated on leaf undersides.
cautions: This symptom pattern still requires regional or laboratory confirmation.

title: Mosaic and distortion may indicate a cucurbit virus
content: Several viruses can affect pumpkins and related squash. Possible signs include puckered or stretched leaves, irregular yellow mosaic patterns, and rings, bumps, or discoloration on fruit. Aphids and cucumber beetles can spread some viruses, but these visual signs are not conclusive.
cautions: Ask a local extension or diagnostic laboratory to distinguish virus injury from other stress.

title: Inspect the stem when pumpkin vines wilt
content: Squash vine borer injury can cause leaves and vines to wilt. A hole and a small pile of sawdust-like material may be visible near the base or lower portion of the main stem where larvae feed inside. Other diseases and water stress can also produce wilting.
cautions: Do not assume all vine wilting is caused by an insect.

title: Bacterial wilt can resemble water stress
content: Cucurbit bacterial wilt may begin with leaves and vines wilting during the day, briefly recovering at night, and eventually collapsing. Striped cucumber beetles are an important carrier. Waterlogged roots, dry soil, stem borers, and other diseases can look similar.
cautions: Seek diagnostic confirmation before attributing wilt to bacteria.

title: Cucumber beetles damage young cucurbits
content: Cucumber beetles may leave irregular, jagged holes in pumpkin leaves and can also chew flowers or stems. Adults are yellow-green with dark stripes or spots. Their feeding matters most on seedlings and young plants, and some beetles can transmit bacterial wilt or viruses.
cautions: Protect pollinator access once flowers open.
Use local integrated-pest-management guidance before considering controls.

title: Base tomato fertilizer choices on soil and fruiting stage
content: For outdoor tomatoes, use a soil test to guide phosphorus and potassium; where extra phosphorus is not recommended, choose a low- or no-phosphorus vegetable fertilizer. A later application may be considered when the first fruits begin enlarging, while compost already added to the soil can reduce the need for more fertilizer.
cautions: Too much nitrogen can produce leafy growth and delay fruiting.
Follow the product label and never use a fertilizer combined with a weed killer around vegetables.

title: Do not auto-recommend fertilizer from a tomato stress report
content: A report that a tomato is stressed or unhealthy does not identify a nutrient need. In the verified case of extreme heat, adding fertilizer promotes growth the plant cannot support and creates additional stress. General fertilizer guidance should therefore wait while the cause of the reported stress remains unknown.
cautions: Leaf color or an image alone does not establish a nutrient deficiency.
Resume fertilizer review only after the stress has been addressed and active growth is appropriate.

title: Use soil evidence and vine development for pumpkin fertilizer
content: Before planting pumpkins, determine fertilizer needs with a soil test and use its recommendations. A general garden fertilizer or well-composted organic amendment may be appropriate when the soil evidence supports it; after vines develop runners, the reviewed guidance supports considering additional nitrogen rather than feeding by an arbitrary calendar.
cautions: Follow the product label and local soil-test recommendations instead of using a fixed app dosage.
Avoid damaging transplant roots because root injury slows establishment and growth.

title: Do not auto-recommend fertilizer from a pumpkin stress report
content: A report that a pumpkin is stressed or unhealthy does not identify a nutrient need. In the verified case of extreme heat, adding fertilizer promotes growth the plant cannot support and creates additional stress. General fertilizer guidance should therefore wait while the cause of the reported stress remains unknown.
cautions: Wilting, leaf color, or an image alone does not establish a nutrient deficiency.
Resume fertilizer review only after the stress has been addressed and active growth is appropriate.

title: Pothos fertilizer is limited to active growth
content: For an indoor pothos in active growth, a balanced houseplant fertilizer may be considered no more often than every other month under the plant-specific guidance. Do not continue the routine when the plant is dormant in winter, and use the product label rather than an app-generated amount.
cautions: Do not exceed the product label.
Slow or absent growth in winter is a reason to wait, not a fertilizer deficiency diagnosis.

title: Wait to fertilize stressed or newly repotted pothos
content: Never fertilize a diseased, injured, or damaged pothos as though fertilizer were medicine; wait for recovery. After repotting, wait at least two to four weeks before regular fertilizing because fresh potting mix commonly contains fertilizer and immediate application is usually unnecessary.
cautions: Excess fertilizer salts can burn roots.
Do not infer fertilizer need from yellow, brown, wilted, or otherwise unhealthy foliage.

title: Snake plants have minimal seasonal fertilizer needs
content: Snake plant fertilizer needs are minimal. During active spring or summer growth, either a broad houseplant fertilizer or a compost-based organic amendment may be considered; slow or dormant growth outside that active period is a reason to wait rather than apply a routine feed.
cautions: Follow the product label and do not exceed it.
Minimal need means a missing or old fertilizer log is not proof that fertilizer is required.

title: Wait to fertilize stressed or newly repotted snake plants
content: Never fertilize a diseased, injured, or damaged snake plant as though fertilizer were medicine; wait for recovery. After repotting, wait at least two to four weeks before regular fertilizing because fresh potting mix commonly contains fertilizer and immediate application is usually unnecessary.
cautions: Excess fertilizer salts can burn roots.
Do not infer fertilizer need from leaf color, damage, wilting, or an image observation.

title: Limit peace lily fertilizer to healthy active growth
content: A peace lily has low fertility needs and fertilizer should be considered only during healthy active growth. Wait when growth is slow or dormant, never use fertilizer as medicine for a diseased or damaged plant, and wait at least two to four weeks after repotting before resuming regular fertilizing.
cautions: Overfertilizing can burn leaf tips and roots.
Use a houseplant product only as its label directs and do not infer need from leaf symptoms.
